SK1053 Use a discard

A named local that exists only to receive a value nobody reads — a return value kept for the call's effect, or an out var the caller does not want.

CategoryModernization
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floorC# 7.0
Since1.3

Why

A name is a claim that something will be referred to again. When nothing refers to it, the name is a small lie the reader has to check: they look for the second use, do not find it, and only then know the call was there for its effect. _ says that in the first character, and it says it to the compiler too — the local stops being allocated and stops being something a later edit can accidentally read.

Example

Instead of:

var ignored = queue.TryDequeue(out var unused);

Write:

_ = queue.TryDequeue(out _);

When it does not fire

⚠ This is not `SK0217`. arrange-discard-declaration decides how an existing discard is spelled — var _ against _ — and never introduces one; this rule introduces one and never restyles one, so the two do not double-count. ⚠ `_` is a discard only where nothing else claims the name. A local, a parameter or a field called _ turns _ = Foo(); into an assignment to that thing, silently, so every lookup for _ at the rewrite position must come back empty. ⚠ Only `out var`, never `out T`. A discard has no type, so replacing an explicitly typed out-variable can change which overload a call resolves to; out var is already typeless in that sense and loses nothing. ⚠ The local's initializer must be a call, a construction, an await or a conditional access — something whose evaluation is the reason the statement exists. var x = 5; is dead code whose repair is deletion, and _ = 5; is the same dead code with an assignment bolted on. ⚠ "Never read" is measured as "never mentioned" over the whole member, deliberately: a later assignment is not a read, but dropping a declaration underneath one is a compile error rather than a tidy-up, and a local written twice and read never has no fix here either way. ⚠ using, await using, const, ref, attributed and multi-declarator declarations are all left alone.
